_note: Rule-change timeline entries chosen for trivia value, plus the 1845 Knickerbocker Rules.

rule_changes.rule: A game used to end after the inning in which a team reached 21 runs. This year it became a nine-inning contest won by the higher score.
Called strikes are introduced — before this, a batter could simply wait for a pitch he liked.
A batter is out on a batted ball, fair or foul, if it is caught on the fly OR after one bounce.
Called balls and bases on balls are introduced.
The one-bounce out on fair balls is abolished; a fair ball must now be caught on the fly.
Bat length is limited to 42 inches — still the limit today.
The batter-runner is allowed to overrun first base.
The batter is officially allowed to call for a high or low pitch (a practice since 1864).
The batter's box is introduced.
Canvas bases 15 inches square are introduced, and home plate is placed in the angle formed by the first- and third-base lines.
It took NINE called balls to draw a walk.
A walk drops to seven called balls, and the batter no longer gets a fourth strike.
Six called balls become a base on balls.
One side of the bat is allowed to be flat — a rule rescinded in 1893.
Four called strikes are adopted — for this season only. Walks are also recorded as hits, also for this season only.
The batter is awarded first base when hit by a pitch.
The strike zone is established between the shoulders and the knees.
Four balls finally become a base on balls — the modern standard.
Large padded mitts are allowed for catchers.
The pitching box is eliminated for a rubber slab, moved from 50 feet to 60 feet 6 inches — the distance still used today.
Foul bunts are classified as strikes.
The infield-fly rule is adopted.
Home plate changes from a square to the five-sided figure used today.
Foul balls start counting as strikes until the batter has two strikes.
The height of the mound is limited to 15 inches above the baselines.
Pitchers are prohibited from soiling a new ball.
All freak deliveries, including the spitball, are outlawed — and RBIs are added to the official score.
A batter is finally credited with a home run if he wins the game in the ninth with a ball hit out of the park.
The minimum home-run distance is set at 250 feet.
The pitcher is allowed to use a rosin bag.
A ball that bounces over the fence now entitles the batter to two bases, not a home run.
The home team must bat second, and the strike zone is redefined as armpits to the top of the knees.
Minimum outfield dimensions are set for all new parks: 325-400-325 feet.
The anti-spitball rule is rewritten and tightened after a wave of moistened pitches the prior season.
The pitcher's mound is dropped five inches and the strike zone shrunk — a direct answer to 1968's Year of the Pitcher. The save also becomes an official rule.
All major-league players are ordered to wear protective helmets.
The American League begins using the designated hitter — on an experimental basis.
The ball is permitted to be covered with cowhide because of a shortage of horses.
Catchers must wear protective helmets while on defense.
Limited instant replay (home run calls, fair or foul) arrives on August 29.
A runner may no longer deviate from his path to initiate contact with the catcher, and the catcher may not block the plate without the ball.
Pitchers no longer throw four intentional balls to issue a walk — the manager just signals the umpire.
A pitcher must face a minimum of three batters, and extra innings begin with a runner on second.
The National League officially adopts the designated hitter.
Bases grow from 15 to 18 inches, defensive shifts are banned, and the pitch clock arrives.

knickerbocker_1845.title: The Knickerbocker Rules (1845)
knickerbocker_1845.note: Alexander J. Cartwright's twenty rules, adopted September 23, 1845 — the foundation of modern baseball.
highlights: 8TH. The game to consist of twenty-one counts, or aces; but at the conclusion an equal number of hands must be played.
9TH. The ball must be pitched, not thrown, for the bat.
10TH. A ball knocked out of the field, or outside the range of the first and third base, is foul.
12TH. If a ball be struck, or tipped, and caught, either flying or on the first bound, it is a hand out.

13TH. A player running the bases shall be out, if the ball is in the hands of an adversary on the base, or the runner is touched with it before he makes his base; it being understood, however, that in no instance is a ball to be thrown at him.
17TH. All disputes and differences relative to the game, to be decided by the Umpire, from which there is no appeal.
